items.title: If something grows at 3% per year, it doubles in 23 years
items.claim: Compound growth at rate r% has a fixed doubling time of about 70/r years (rule of 70) or 72/r (rule of 72). The doubling time doesn't change as the quantity grows. That's what 'exponential' means — proportional rate, not larger jumps.
items.prompt: Why is the doubling time constant?

options.text: For exponential growth dN/dt = kN, N(t) = N0 * e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k. Independent of N0 — the time to go from 1 to 2 equals the time to go from 1000 to 2000
Only applies to populations of bacteria

items.reveal:
Exponential growth: dN/dt = k * N. Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k.

Rule of 70/72: if k% per period, doubling time ≈ 70/k (or 72/k) periods. At 7%/year, doubles in ~10 years. At 1%/year, doubles in ~70 years. At 0.5%/year (current global population growth), doubles in ~140 years.

Exponential growth is unrealistic for long times — no real system maintains constant growth rate forever. The logistic model corrects: dN/dt = k * N * (1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity.

Logistic solution: N(t) = K / (1 + ((K - N_0)/N_0) * e^(-kt)). Starts exponential (when N << K), saturates at K.

Applications:
- Epidemics: early growth (susceptible >> infected) is exponential; saturates as susceptibles deplete (or interventions take effect). The famous 'flatten the curve' is intervening in this growth equation.
- Populations: many wild populations roughly logistic. Carrying capacity set by food, predation, disease.
- Innovation diffusion: technology adoption (smartphones, electric cars) often logistic.
- Tumour growth: early stages can be exponential; later stages limited by blood supply.

Misinterpretations:
- 'Exponential' is loosely used to mean 'fast growth'. Mathematically, it means proportional growth. A linear quantity can grow faster than an exponential one in the short term.
- Confusing exponential growth (rate proportional to value) with super-exponential (faster than any fixed exponential).
- Underestimating doubling times. Many people fail the 'penny doubling' problem: a penny doubled daily for 30 days becomes ~10 million dollars.
items.why: Exponential growth feels like 'fast growth'. Mathematically it's something specific: constant percentage rate, constant doubling time. Understanding doubling times is key to understanding epidemics, populations, finance, and Moore's law.

items.title: Matrices don't commute — and that's why quantum mechanics works
items.claim: AB is not generally equal to BA for matrices. The order of operations matters. This isn't a defect — it's the most important feature of matrix algebra and the mathematical foundation of quantum uncertainty.

options.text: Matrices represent linear transformations of vectors; applying transformation A then B is generally not the same as B then A. The non-commutativity reflects that composition of transformations in higher dimensions does NOT commute in general
AB = BA always works for invertible matrices

items.reveal:
For matrices, AB and BA are generally different — and AB is well-defined only when A's columns equal B's rows. Even for square matrices of the same size, AB and BA can differ wildly.

Example: A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Different.

When does AB = BA? Some special cases: scalar multiples of identity; same diagonal matrix; simultaneously diagonalisable matrices; powers of the same matrix.

The commutator [A, B] = AB - BA measures the non-commutativity. For ordinary numbers it's always zero; for matrices it can be anything.

In QUANTUM MECHANICS:
- Physical observables are represented as matrices (or operators on Hilbert space).
- The commutator of position and momentum: [x, p] = i * hbar. Non-zero!
- Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the variance of two non-commuting observables, in any state, has a lower bound proportional to the commutator. You can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely.

This is not a measurement limitation — it's a structural feature of the math. Eigenvectors of non-commuting matrices are different; states have to choose between definite x and definite p.

Lie groups and algebras: continuous symmetry transformations form groups whose generators are matrices with commutation relations. The group SU(3) underlies the strong nuclear force; SU(2) describes weak force and quantum spin; U(1) describes electromagnetism. The standard model of particle physics is built from non-commuting matrices.

In computer graphics: rotation matrices in 3D don't commute (mentioned in another card). The order matters when composing transformations.
items.why: Multiplication seems naturally commutative. For matrices it isn't — and the depth of this fact is that quantum mechanics, particle physics, computer graphics, and most of modern physics rely on it.

items.title: Tilting your phone changes things differently depending on the order
items.claim: Take a book. Rotate 90 degrees about its vertical axis, then 90 degrees about its horizontal axis. Now reset and reverse the order: horizontal first, then vertical. The book ends up in a DIFFERENT orientation. Rotations in 3D do not commute.

options.text: Rotation matrices in 3D are non-commutative — R1 * R2 is not equal to R2 * R1 in general. SO(3) is a non-abelian Lie group, unlike rotations in 2D which DO commute

items.reveal:
Rotations in 2D (the plane): R(theta1) * R(theta2) = R(theta1 + theta2) = R(theta2) * R(theta1). They commute. The group SO(2) is abelian.

Rotations in 3D: not commutative. The group SO(3) is non-abelian. The order in which you apply rotations changes the final orientation.

Experiment: rotate book 90° about vertical (y-axis) — left becomes back. Then rotate 90° about (now front-pointing) x-axis — back becomes bottom. Reset. Now rotate 90° about x first — top becomes back. Then 90° about y — back becomes left. Final orientations differ.

Mathematically: if R_x is rotation about x-axis and R_y about y-axis, R_x R_y is not equal to R_y R_x. The 'commutator' [R_x, R_y] = R_x R_y - R_y R_x is non-zero, representing a small rotation about the third axis.

Consequences:
- Aerospace: gimbal lock — a 3-axis gyroscope can have its three rotation axes align such that one rotational degree of freedom is lost. Famously almost killed Apollo astronauts on Apollo 11.
- Quaternions (Hamilton 1843) parametrise 3D rotations without gimbal lock and are standard in 3D graphics.
- Quantum mechanics: angular momentum operators have the same commutation structure as 3D rotations, leading to quantisation.

In higher dimensions (n > 3), rotation groups SO(n) are also non-commutative.
items.why: Rotation seems like a simple geometric concept. In 3D it's surprisingly subtle — the order matters, and that fact has cost lives, structured quantum mechanics, and shaped every video game engine.
